You turn the table.
By taking this action of hunting all those masks
and archetype characters that we play,
you're actually taking the action of being the hunter.
And by being the hunter, you're developing the attitude, the point of view of the hunter, or what the Toltecs call the stalker.
In that process, you're creating a new character that you live by.
We'll call it the hunter.
We can also call it the warrior, the spiritual warrior that is freeing himself or herself from all these dreams of reaction.
Take a look at the point of views you've been looking at things from.
And now take them and be much more specific into the region of each of those points of view in terms of masks and archetype characters and attitudes.
Continue with that hunting your attention process where we go far beyond just looking at the point of view we take on.
And now we break down that point of view into very specific archetype characters and masks,
and we take an inventory and write out the specifics of each of those characters that we play.
Now we're really getting into scouting the other team.
Before, when you were hunting your attention, it was just about learning that that ball game
and that play for your attention was going on.
And if you did that assignment, you know how difficult it is to keep your attention.
It's not easy.
Well, this is the next step of that assignment, to help you master all those places where your point of view gets hooked and where it goes.
And by doing this, by becoming aware and observing all these different masks,
you are helping to master and hold your attention outside of their grasp.
Good luck, and may you become a great hunter.
As an additional part of this homework,
once you've outlined these different cast of characters that you have,
or as you're in the progress of outlining them,
I want you to combine this exercise with the exercise from the autobiography.
which was the second session.
And I want you to write about yourself in third person,
and I want you to write about what goes on in your mind
in reference to these different characters that you see,
or what goes on in your behaviors
in reference to these different characters that you see.
So that you'll be writing, say, about yourself,
referring to yourself as he.
He then went to see this person to tell him this,
and while he was walking over there, his judge was commenting in his mind.
His victim was commenting in his mind.
Or in retrospect, he could see that it was his hero that was inspired to go do this
because of a motivation to get approval or get some kind of reward out of this.
What you're doing by doing this is you're allowing to take one step further back in being a witness.
In the autobiography, what you're doing is you're stepping back from your mind.
In this exercise, you're taking two steps back from your mind,
because you're watching your mind in your head and you're watching the individual aspects of your mind.
This is giving you a much further removed viewpoint to help you stay in the observer frame
and stay out of reaction. So combine the two,
write in third person about what character archetypes you play out during the week
or during this past month,
or wherever you have an emotional reaction, and
in that writing out of the events of the day or the week,
write about the archetypes and the masks that are at play
as you had those experiences.

Pathway to Happiness

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/07-characters

                                                                        May 8, 2019




07 Characters

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community


Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/pmv7LGv8WEY

Characters lesson audio

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Character lesson audio. You may find it helpful to listen multiple
times.

2. Write out a list of your cast of characters as you find them. Don’t worry
about getting them “right”. This list will evolve and change as you become more aware.
You can come back to it periodically and revise your list.

3. Journal about the different characters of your personality, emotions,
behaviors, and thoughts. This replaces the Third Person journal writing
practice. You can go back to the writings you did in third person about yourself and
look for aspects of characters to help you find them. This will help you more clearly
separate your Conscious Self from the different false identities your belief system has
created about you.

Some notes

You might begin by going back to some of your third person writing and looking at
patterns to. Points of view/perspectives, or consistent emotions, or the same thoughts
over and over will be a clue to a character. By having done the third person writing, and
spending time looking at your behavior from this perspective it should be easier to see
these types of character patterns.

At this point it is not important to “get this assignment right”. Just by looking for them
you are accomplishing being a more skilled observer. There are many creative ways to
describe the different parts of our personality so there really is no “right” way or

                                                                                                                                   1/5

“wrong” way. That means you have some creative license here to organize what you find
however you like.

Here are some things these characters might come up with about this assignment that
you can write about. These are just some examples that may or may not apply to you.
Begin building a detailed description of each.

The perfectionist will want to get this assignment “right”. Write about that guy and
what his agenda is.

The Victim will be afraid of getting this assignment wrong or screwing it up. Write
about her, and what she is afraid of.

The Judge will tell you that you are doing it wrong, or that it wont’ be right. Write
about that character and the things it says and thinks. You might include the
motivations about what it is trying to do, and what it is afraid you will fail at.

There might be a procrastinator that wants to put this off til later. Write about him
now. He is telling you something about part of your mind and the way it works against
your well being.

There might be a character in there that thinks that it has it all figured out
and doesn’t need to write. That “you” (meaning her) can do it in “her” head just by
thinking about it. That “she” can keep it all straight and so it doesn’t need to be written
down.

Then as you do your journal writing each day, make note of what the characters are
saying, thinking, feeling, and how they are behaving.

This writing about these aspects of your personality is developing your observer skills,
as well as your skepticism skills, as well as shifting your perspective away from the
beliefs in the mind about your self. A lot of separate benefits at the same time.

Resistance to change

Common responses include but are not limited to:

      I won’t know who I am if I don’t have these aspects.
      I won’t exist if I don’t have these.
      I won’t be able to express myself if I let these go?

The emotions that come up will be confusion about “Who am I?” and feelings of fear
about not existing.

These responses are normal. You are challenging how your mind has defined you, the
term “I”, “me”, and everything about your identity. You might say that beliefs about
your identity are the biggest core beliefs you have. When you change these, everything


                                                                                                                                   2/5

moves a lot easier. It’s just that there is probably a lot of thoughts, emotions, and faith
connecting you to these beliefs about “I” dentity. That’s okay, they can be changed
through lots of small steps.

Start by writing in third person all these resistance thoughts. Later you might see these
are coming from character identities.

There might be a fear about where you can write this so that it will be a secret and
nobody can read it. A journal isn’t safe, and a laptop isn’t safe. This character is afraid
of what others would think of us if they knew what kinds of things we were thinking and
doing. That’s okay to have that kind of character. And it is okay to find something safe
to write in that is password protected.

These are not the kinds of thoughts or explorations that we want others to know that we
have. They are often characterized in the most detrimental way as some psychological
disorder. They are not that. They are quite normal. Just ask any one that has sat down
to meditate. All people have minds that do incessant thinking, including Buddhist
monks, until they don’t.

Most people have voices in their head. It’s not a problem because they are not
dangerous so they don’t need diagnosis and a label (PS diagnosis and labels don’t
actually help them change.) The people that don’t “hear” voices, just assume that all
that chatter is their own thinking. The thoughts that keep them up at night when they
are trying to sleep, they claim are their thoughts. This assumption seems plausible until
you ask them to turn off their own thinking. When you can’t turn it off, and on at will,
then it isn’t you consciously thinking. IT is then that what you are hearing are the
thoughts from your unconscious mind.

The mind quiets with practice, and faster than a monk’s, when you inventory these
thoughts and characters in the manner you are learning to do here.

Common questions

It feels like I won't exist if I get rid of these characters?
The feeling “I wont’ exist” might better be described as fear. The story or thought is “I
feel I won’t exist.” Or it might be a different emotion. Either way be as specific as you
can about what the feeling is. Then attribute that feeling and thought to a character.
Give it an identity other than “I” or “me”.

It is a feeling that is coming from some belief. That belief won’t exist if you separate
from it. The fear belongs to that belief.

It seems like there are an endless number of characters. Is that possible?
If you attribute a different character to every thought then there can be 20,000
characters a day. That’s too many to manage for this process.



                                                                                                                                   3/5

To help manage look for patterns of attitude and emotion. All anger and frustration
responses might be one character. Feelings of powerless, overwhelm, and helplessness
is a different character. A character that just narrates events with no emotion, is a
different one.

 Grouping thoughts this way will give you a manageable amount. A manageable
amount of characters is probably 12-20. Maybe some people can handle more than that,
or some people like less to work with. If your mind is getting overwhelmed, then take a
couple characters and merge them so you have fewer.

Again, the hunting is more important than being accurate with the labels. This is about
heightening your observer skills, and not so much about accuracy of labels.

How do I know if I am naming my characters correctly and getting this right?
So with this question it sounds as if there is a character that is concerned, about getting
it “right” or afraid of getting it wrong. Maybe one of each. Attribute this thought to one
of your characters, or make up one that you can attribute these thoughts and feelings
to.

The intent of the exercise is to separate YOU as awareness and consciousness from the
parts of your mind that are belief patterns. So the concern is not about getting it
“right”.

Simply by attributing a lot of these thoughts and emotions to the automatic patterns of
the mind you will be successfully separating your sense of identity. That is success.

You can get the characters mixed up, cross them over at times, mis-label what the judge
does as the victim etc, and you will still be successfully separating your mind from your
Conscious Observer self.

So, give yourself the freedom to not get this “right” and get the benefits anyways. With
time you will get more clarity on the details of characters and move them around to
different places.

What if I am not sure which character is responsible for a thought or emotion?
Guess. Make your best guess, and go with that. Later if you find more emotions and
beliefs that reveal more about that character, and you likely will, you change it.

Think of this as first draft. There will be some iterations of realizations. There can also
be some blind spots. You might also be working on some of your beliefs in two months
with some other practices and decide for a specific issue, to make a new character that is
specific to that issue.

These are tools for you to use to organize all those beliefs, thoughts, emotions, and
behaviors. You can change the organization at any time in a way that suits you better.

Supporting videos
                                                                                                                                   4/5

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/Oh2zAQCdYLU

What is the Ego?

The ego is the collection of characters of the mind. The ego can hijack your identity and
trick you into behaving on its behalf instead of your own. You can also look at it as
formidable opponent, that you can learn from through training with it in a respectful
way.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/n6F3GPiOyE0

Not all characters are bad

Some are mixed. Stubbornness can be a good characteristic when applied well.

Make a list of your ally characters also. Practice being aware of them. Over time you will
be able to move in and out of them consciously to help assist you.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/VDkhqk3zPpU

Resistance from your characters is normal.

What would you expect them to do? Here is how to handle it.





                                                                                                                                   5/5

07 Characters Transcript

   pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/07-characters/07-characters-transcript

                                                                        May 11, 2019

The topic of this session is “Hunting your cast of characters”. This is very much a
mindfulness exercise. And it’s a very active one. And as we’re successful in it we’re going
to do a lot of self-discovery. This is a process that’s just going to continue. Something
that I what you to practice as you do this exercise is to specifically continue with the
“Acceptance” exercise. Particularly in this process of self discovery, there are many
opportunities for the Judge in our mind to use this level of new found awareness to
judge ourselves, to criticize ourselves, to put ourselves down or find something wrong
with ourselves. This is one of the principal reactions that we have with the Judge. And
it’s why I’ve given you the “Acceptance” exercise. I want you to practice that exercise
with your new found awareness in this process, and I talk about going one step beyond
in this lesson by going from acceptance all the way to gratitude. If you can’t get to
gratitude, at least practice acceptance.

Something that I want you to notice throughout this session is that I talk about these
different aspects of our personality and I work to clearly identify them as aspects of our
personality, as character archetypes or such. What I’m inviting, encouraging you to do
is to develop a sense of yourself that is independent of these different aspects of your
personality, to identify yourself as being the witness-consciousness, the Observer, that
we talked about in previous sessions, and to notice that these aspects of our personality
are just masks or characters that we put on for a moment, express ourselves a certain
way, and then take them off. They are not permanent pictures of what we are. They are
just different ways of expressing ourselves. And so in this way I clearly differentiate that
there’s “us”, this conscious awareness, and then there is this “personality” that may
change in every moment, but that personality is not “us”, it’s not our authentic self. So,
that’s the differentiation I make in this and I’m asking you to be aware of it as I talk
about it in this session, so that you can practice being aware of it in this exercise.

One of the things that was kind of fun about editing this session I realized at the end of
it, I have talked a lot about this in a very Hunter, Spiritual Warrior manner, and I
realized that this goes back to a lot of the old ways that my mentor don Miguel used to
teach, and I hope you’d enjoy it, it’s very direct challenge, but at the same time you don’t
have to take it that way. Just understand that’s one style, one approach of a certain
attitude you can take about this, but you can also approach it any way you choose.

So good luck, have fun, happy hunting.

This is an assignment I refer to as “Hunting our cast of characters”. What do I mean by
“cast of characters”? If we go back to one of our recent assignments about being
aware of our point of view, being aware of where our attention goes, that assignment
leads into this one. That assignment we began sitting on a court in that ball game and

                                                                                                                           1/10

watching the ideas fly in our mind, watching the ways the different voices try to hook
our attention and to pull us into a story, or maybe people in the outside world hook our
attention and pull us into a story, whether it’d be a salesman, or a relative, or a friend –
they want us to hear their story. Well, we have all sorts of characters that run around in
our own mind. In that mitote, that internal dialogue, that cacophony of voices, we’ve
got all sorts of different folks speaking to us all the time. Two very obvious ones: the
Judge and the Victim. Miguel Ruiz refers to those in the book “The Four Agreements”.
Judge – always there, always critical, always raising something up above something
else, or always putting something down below something else, or somebody else. And
the Victim is literally accepting all the criticisms, all the unworthiness. We’ve also got to
expose the Victim somewhat in our “Abdication of Power” stories. You’ve come to see
perhaps one of the stories that the Victim tells and through that got to identify that
character a little more clearly. That that’s the part of our mind, part of our sub
personality that buys into that kind of story that somebody is doing something to me, or
them living their lives and that character interprets it as “Oh, it’s because of me,
they are doing it against me,” when in fact they are just living their lives, they are
just doing what they do. Ok, so, if we have the Judge personality going in our mind, and
we have the Victim personality going in our mind, who else might be there? Are we just
limited to those two? My experience is no, we are not. We’ve got other aspects of our
personality, and they play out in various ways. And they play out in two words:

1) The world of the imagination, in our mind: the way we imagine ourselves, the way
we interpret things, the way we run our internal dialogue in our own mind, what point
of view we take on things internally – that is one way that we play these characters. And
when I say “characters”, these are characters or attitudes we take on, these are sub
personalities, we can also call “archetypes of our behavior”, certain aspects of our
behavior. Do we play the same character all the time? No, we don’t.

2) The second area that we play out these characters is in the external world. And
some of those characters are what is our predominant attitude in the business meeting,
what is our predominant attitude in business, what is our attitude about money, what is
our personality towards our children or towards our parents. So we play different roles
for different people. We are not the same person for our mom and dad that we are for
our children. We bring a certain attitude to our children, we bring a certain attitude to
our mom and dad, or to our friends, or to our lover. There’re certain aspects of
ourselves that we are most comfortable with in certain environments. That’s on the
external side of things. Is it wrong or good, or bad that we play different roles? No. This
is just the way we were conditioned to be. The question is: “Are we aware of it?” And if
we are not aware of it, how are those behavior automatic and how do they pull us into
the situations, dramas, emotions that we don’t wanna be in? How does a certain
character archetype that we play pull us into a cascading series of emotion?

So, identifying the characters we play, the attitudes of the archetypes we envision
ourselves in, whether it be in the external world or in the internal world of our mind
and how we interpret things, is the key to seeing the whole patterns of our behavior. It’s

                                                                                                                           2/10

one thing to break one agreement, find the agreement and say: “Ok, with this person I
do that and I’m not going to do that anymore,” but if we are going to change our lives, a
much faster way to do it is to notice how we play a certain role, and then to notice all the
different places we play that role in all sorts of different situations. So that we can erase
an entire pattern, instead of changing just one agreement with one person. If we can
modify that whole archetype character, we change that behavior pattern everywhere in
our lives, so we can make much faster changes, more profound changes, if we start
looking at huge patterns instead of individual interactions. And this is what we’re going
to do.

The characters that we play, and I may refer to them as archetype characters, as
personalities, sub personalities, probably the best word to define them or describe
them, to differentiate them one from the other is to look at them as attitudes. Some
attitudes are very determined, some attitudes are very deserving, some attitudes are
very heroic, are “Got to go save the day” type of attitudes, some attitudes are very
 nurturing, some are loving, some are comedian – they are fun, they are playful. These
are different aspects, different ways that we express ourselves.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to identify and list your whole cast of
characters that you play, both in the outside world and the ones you run as yourself in
your own imagination. I’m not going to give you a guideline or a list of what characters
to look for. This is for you to notice on your own, see all the different ways you express
yourself or you interpret things, identify those points of view or those attitudes, and
then write out the role sheet, take each one of those characters, say for instance the
Judge, write up the places that it shows up, the types of things that it judges, where it
jumps in, how it interacts, what kinds of emotions and attitudes it brings when it shows
up, does it play mostly internally or is it outwardly expressed, does it criticize a lot on
yourself or does it criticize a lot on other people, what is the structure of its arguments,
what’s the nature of its personality. Same thing with the Victim: where does it show up,
who or what kind of people is it most commonly out to play, where is it you most feel
you are in that role and what do you do from there: are you quiet, are you hiding, do
you put a big mask over to cover it up, and then what is that mask that you use to cover
it up. So what mask or role do you put over that Victim to cover it up, so that other
people don’t see that you’re afraid, or timid or else, or you come out and show people
that. These are the different ways we hide ourselves using other characters. As far as the
other ones you might look for – I’m not going to give you a list. This is for you to be
creative, be wide open, call them whatever you like. You can give them silly names, you
can be Vinnie the Victim and Jeremiah the Judge, or the Hanging Judge, or Judge Roy
Bean, which is the hanging judge. Give them funny names if you like, be creative. At the
end of this assignment you should have a list of characters at least about 6 long, try to
keep it no more than a dozen. If you find yourself getting more than a dozen, start to
combine them and see if some of the attributes can be collected under one type of
character, so that you don’t have a list of 83. 83 is a little difficult to manage. You’ll find
out that a lot of them have similar tendencies and we can start to group them under one
general character. So you should have somewhere between 6 and 12. If you have more –

                                                                                                                           3/10

no penalties, no Judge is going to come out and get you, unless you will send your own.
So with your list of characters you’re then going to write out what are the attributes of
each, when does it come out, what kind of environment, who with. If you’ve been to the
play and you looked at the beginning of the play, there has the list of characters right
there in the beginning. And it gives a little brief outline into that person’s background or
history, or what role they’ll be playing. This is what we are going to do. We are going to
write an outline on each one of our sub-personalities, each one of the masks we wear,
when we wear it and perhaps maybe why we wear it, if you can spot that.

What’s interesting to note is that these characters are neither good nor bad, they are not
right or wrong, it’s not that we should or shouldn’t be playing them. This is more about
being honest and saying: “Ok, this is what we do. These are the roles we play.”
This assignment is not for your Judge to get a hold of and say: “Oh, this character is bad,
I shouldn’t be playing this one,” or “This one is great, I should this one more.” No. This
is not your Judge helping you to your self-improvement or your happiness. Just
dissolving one character is a pretty minor way to go about it, and actually your Judge
doesn’t really have the power to dissolve the characters, so don’t worry about it. It has
the capacity to give a story of condemnation, but not actually make anything go away,
no matter how much you believe it. These characters aren’t good or bad, they are just
what we do. And we’ve been doing them for years, we’ve been doing them out of
automatic profiles of what we’ve learned in domestication of behavior.

Sometimes I will see a character starts to be created in the grocery store. If I see a mom
with a child, and the child is 3 years old and wants a candy bar. That child will have a
temper tantrum and berate or cry, or feel sorry for itself, and cringe away and hide from
mom, so that mom feels rejected. Those are whole emotional dynamics, maybe more
than one, trying to tug our mom’s emotions to get that candy bar. If we find ourselves
doing such a things at times, we can call that character the Temper Tantrum Child. It’s
an attitude, it’s behavior we take on, that we learned years ago, not knowing why we
learned it.

We can see another character we could play if we just look at children. They want that
candy bar, they come up and they are all affectionate and loving, and snuggling up with
mom, and they really: “Mom, please, I love you, can I have a candy bar?” Well,
they are a Sweet Talker, they are hooking someone’s attention just to get what they
want. They do love they mom, and they are just using that time, to give that certain
expression, cause it works for their benefit. Nothing wrong with that, it helps them get
what they want, if it works – great, if it doesn’t work – great, but when do we do it? Do
we want to be doing it? Do we have a choice to play that role? It may be fine that we
get what we want – nobody’s harmed. The question is whether this is the way we want
to build our relationships. You know, until we recognize we play this role and we start to
refrain from the habit of it, we don’t have an opportunity to do something else. It’s like
that role pulls us into that dream, we play that role automatically, and don’t notice. Well





                                                                                                                           4/10

without awareness of that habituation we don’t have the opportunity to make a different
choice. We need to see it, identify it, say: “Ok, do I want to keep doing that?”, “Now that
I see it there, do I want to keep doing that?”

Another kind of character – Comedian – someone who’s fun, someone who’s playful,
who’s a life of the party. Nothing wrong with that – you’re having a great time. The
question is whether there’s another side to that character. Is there a side to that
character that is needy of attention? If they don’t get a certain response or feedback
from people, how does that character feel? So, Comedian can be great, beautiful, fun, an
expression of just great joy, or it could also have at the same time an expression
underneath it that is needful of attention and does it to get love from other people. Then
the Comedian, the Clown character – it’s a character that is neither good nor bad, but
what is it’s nature? What is its driving influence? What is the attitude behind that
expression? What are the needs of that character? These are the insights that I want you
to look into in your cast of characters. And you can look into it, into the Judge, the
Clown, or whatever other aspects of personality you find.

I gave this assignment to a client, and he runs his own business. And what he found was
he has a character that he called the King. Well, the King is a kind of person he found
out is right, gives the orders, and doesn’t want to be questioned. And if anybody gives a
dissenting opinion, he wants to send in his troops and squash it. He doesn’t want any
dissension. He wants his word to be law. That’s his King. And he found out that that
King, while being a wonderful provider for people’s income and livelihood in his
kingdom of the office, that King also has an attitude of a tyrant. So there’s a benevolent
side to the King, while he really looks after his people, and there’s a tyrannical side to
his King, where he wants to squash things, if things don’t go just his way. Does it come
out all the time? No, lot of times he finds himself biting his lip. Well, when he looked at
the King, he found other aspects and stories and characters internal, that were
supporting the King: he found the Judge in there that would judge other people, he
found the Victim in there that felt betrayed because his employees didn’t appreciate
what he was trying to do. He felt unappreciated and the Judge turned around and
looked there and said: “Hey, they are not seeing what I’m doing for them, they have no
gratitude, they don’t appreciate me, they have no respect for me, they are wrong in the
way that they are looking at this, this is their problem.” Well you see that that attitude of
not being appreciated as a Victim rolled into an attitude of “what they are doing is
wrong, they don’t have enough gratitude.” And the King was part of the attitude that felt
supreme, felt like “Ok, I am really right, I am justified in doing this, because I provide so
much for these people.” Well, those were three attitudes, you can say three different
 characters in one instance, in one reaction. They went very quick. How he found it is
he first started just by noticing this attitude of supremacy, but as he spent time and
really wrote out what that character looked like, he noticed that the Judge behind it was
casting all his judgments on his employees for their poor attitudes, their lack of
appreciation. Well, he felt that that story that he’s not appreciated was a betrayal and
that was a Victim attitude. Three masks, all layered on top of each other, all coming out
in one reaction.

                                                                                                                           5/10

You know some times when we get upset people ask: “What are you feeling?” And it’s
hard for to describe. Well, often it’s hard to describe because we are having
 multiple reactions at once. And it’s hard to get down to the whole structure of the
agreements that are driving this reaction. In this man’s case he had a reaction of feeling
betrayed and not appreciated, and that was from the Victim mask, and then he had the
feeling that what these people are doing is wrong so it was sense of righteousness and
anger that was coming from this tyrannical King. So he had (1) betrayed, (2)
righteousness and (3) anger – all three of them together. And if we ask someone who’s
feeling all that: “How do you feel?”, and we aren’t really practiced in noticing the subtle
details, a lot of times we’ll say: “I just feel stinky”, “I don’t feel good”, “I am not happy”.
And that’s very general. And if we’re going sort up these underlying agreements and
behavior dynamics, it’s much easier to do if we pull them apart, break them out into
